title: BART Transbay Tube Seismic Retrofit Bolts Fail, Audit Blames Oversight
text:
Hundreds of high‑strength anchor bolts used in BART's Transbay Tube seismic retrofit snapped during installation, reaching 30% failure in 2019. An audit links the failures to flawed oversight, a material substitution, and insufficient quality control, forcing $2 million in replacements and doubling the fastening budget.
When installed, 30 percent of the high strength bolts failed in the first half of 2019, according to the report. Hundreds of high-strength bolts used in BART ’s Transbay Tube seismic retrofit project snapped during installation.
Investigative Reporter Jaxon Van Derbeken reports. Hundreds of high strength anchor bolts needed to secure seismic plates on the retrofit of BART’s Transbay Tube failed immediately – a breakdown that a new audit blames on flawed oversight by BART.
In the end, more than 8,000 bolts – originally ordered to fasten the steel plates that were installed to help the tunnel withstand seismic motions – had to be replaced with different anchors, at a total cost of more than $2 million – twice the originally budgeted amount for the fastening system, the audit found. The project was finished in 2024.
A year earlier, an apparent insider complained to the BART Office of the Inspector General, alleging quality control and oversight lapses on the $313 million project. The inspector general’s audit report noted that back in 2018, BART authorized one of the retrofit contractors to substitute Korean-made steel for the U.S. steel originally specified for the bolts, because of the contractor’s supply concerns.
BART agreed but told the contractor the Korean bolt material had be tested to assure it met specific chemical composition standards and completed with welding and quality control specifications. The BART inspector general’s probe found the bolts were ordered and manufactured nearly a year before BART got the detailed plan as to how they would inspected and tested.
“As a result, BART did not have the opportunity to evaluate planned welding processes and quality control measures,” according to the audit. When installed, 30 percent of the high strength bolts failed in the first half of 2019, according to the report. The subsequent investigation revealed that quality assurance efforts turned out to be far less robust than BART had wanted.
Just three out of 8,030 anchors were tested, according to the audit, and those tests were done on only one of the two types of bolts BART’s contractor had ordered. In the end, BART scrapped the anchor design and required the removal of the 8,000+ bolts that had cost more than $1 million to make. Replacing them with a redesigned system cost BART another $1 million. The report faulted BART for not enforcing its existing policies.
The tests done on the materials from Korea did not find the product to be inferior, according to Inspector General Claudette Biemeret.
“Rather than continue to press the issue and shift the burden to the contractor,” Biemeret said, “BART decided to pay for a different method and scrap the original anchors. ” In a statement, BART said that after the original bolt failures, the agency developed an alternative design that eliminated the welded connection and still met the project's seismic engineering requirements. The redesign anchors were installed without failure, BART said.
“We appreciate the Office of Inspector General’s rigorous and independent oversight that is helping to make BART better,” BART said in its statement.
